name: qa_training_pairs.json
description: 55 question/answer training pairs for retrieval and fine-tuning. Answers never promise profit.
format: Each item: q (user question), a (ideal answer), tags. Use for retrieval or fine-tuning. Answers never promise profit.

pairs.q: What is a Deriv Volatility Index?
pairs.a: A synthetic index generated by an algorithm at a fixed annualised volatility (V75 = 75%). It is not the CBOE VIX. It trades 24/7, is not driven by news, and Deriv is the counterparty on CFDs.

pairs.q: Which Volatility Index is best for beginners?
pairs.a: V10 or V25 on H1/H4 are usually suggested because moves are slower and stops are easier to manage. Start on demo with 0.25-0.5% risk.

pairs.q: Does higher volatility mean more profit?
pairs.a: No. Higher volatility means larger stops, smaller position size and faster losses. Size must shrink as volatility rises.

pairs.q: What is the difference between V75 and V75 (1s)?
pairs.a: The 1s version produces a tick every second, so it has more ticks with smaller individual moves; the standard version ticks about every two seconds with larger moves. Both target the same annual volatility.

pairs.q: Give me a simple trend strategy for V75.
pairs.a: On M15/H1: long when price is above EMA50 and EMA200 and EMA20 is above EMA50, price pulls back to EMA20/50 and a bullish rejection candle closes; stop below the pullback low with an ATR buffer; target 1.5-2R; trail after 1R. Mirror for shorts. Treat it as a hypothesis and backtest it first.

pairs.q: How do I size a trade?
pairs.a: Position size = (equity x risk%) / stop distance (in value per point). Example: equity 1000, risk 1% = 10, stop 10 points at 1 per point -> size 1. Choose the stop first, then size.

pairs.q: How much should I risk per trade?
pairs.a: Common guidance is 0.25-1% while learning, with a hard cap around 2%. Use the low end on very volatile indices.

pairs.q: What is a good risk-reward ratio?
pairs.a: At least 1.5R for trend trades. The break-even win rate is 1/(1+RR): 40% at RR 1.5, 33% at RR 2, 50% at RR 1, before costs.

pairs.q: What is expectancy?
pairs.a: Average result per trade: win_rate x average_win - loss_rate x average_loss. A strategy needs positive expectancy after spread, slippage and swaps.

pairs.q: What are Drift Switch Indices?
pairs.a: Synthetic indices (DSI 10, 20, 30) that cycle through bullish drift, bearish drift and sideways regimes. The number is the average minutes between switches, not a countdown.

pairs.q: How do I trade DSI?
pairs.a: Trade with the regime after confirmation: EMA20 and EMA50 aligned, higher highs/lows, enter on a pullback, stop beyond the swing, and exit before the average regime duration ends. Skip choppy periods, risk 0.5-1% or less, and stop after 2-3 losses. No profit is guaranteed.

pairs.q: Which DSI should I start with?
pairs.a: DSI 30 on M5/M15 since it switches less often and gives more time to analyse.

pairs.q: Will a DSI switch happen exactly every 10 minutes?
pairs.a: No. 10 is an average. Switches can come sooner or later, so never trade to a stopwatch.

pairs.q: What is stop-and-reverse on DSI?
pairs.a: Close a long when the bullish regime breaks (price below EMA20 then EMA50) and only go short after bearish confirmation (lower high, strong bearish close, price below both EMAs). If unclear, stay flat.

pairs.q: What are Crash and Boom indices?
pairs.a: Synthetic indices that drift slowly in one direction and spike in the other. Boom drifts down with upward spikes; Crash drifts up with downward spikes. The number is the average ticks between spikes.

pairs.q: Is a Boom spike 'due' after a long wait?
pairs.a: No. Spike arrival is treated as memoryless, so waiting longer does not raise the probability. Thinking otherwise is the gambler's fallacy.

pairs.q: Can a stop-loss fail on Crash/Boom?
pairs.a: Yes, spikes can jump past a stop, so the actual loss can exceed the planned loss. Use small size.

pairs.q: Do indicators work on synthetic indices?
pairs.a: Deriv says that with no order book, historical patterns on most synthetics can be coincidental, and technical analysis is most defensible on Range Break indices. Indicator strategies must be tested; do not assume they work.

pairs.q: What is a Range Break index?
pairs.a: An index that oscillates between support and resistance and then breaks out at random times. Channel analysis can be more meaningful there than on other synthetics.

pairs.q: What is correlation?
pairs.a: A number from -1 to +1 showing how consistently two return series move together: +1 same direction, 0 no linear link, -1 opposite.

pairs.q: Positive vs negative correlation strategies?
pairs.a: Positive correlation: trend confirmation, sector rotation, correlation-aware sizing and pairs trading. Negative correlation: diversification and hedging.

pairs.q: What is correlation divergence?
pairs.a: When two assets break their usual relationship: positively correlated assets separate, or negatively correlated assets move together. Traders either bet on convergence or treat it as a regime change and follow the stronger move.

pairs.q: How do I run a pairs trade?
pairs.a: Pick two logically related, correlated assets (rolling corr above ~0.7), confirm the spread is stationary or cointegrated, compute the spread z-score using the hedge ratio, enter at about +/-2, exit near 0, stop near 3-3.5 or on correlation breakdown, and time-stop at 2-3x half-life.

pairs.q: Why use returns instead of prices for correlation?
pairs.a: Prices that trend can look correlated by accident (spurious correlation). Returns remove most of the trend and give a more reliable measure.

pairs.q: Does correlation imply causation?
pairs.a: No. Two assets can move together because of a shared driver, coincidence or a market-wide factor.

pairs.q: Are Deriv synthetic indices correlated with each other?
pairs.a: Separate synthetic generators are expected to be essentially independent, so cross-index correlation should be near zero. Measure it before assuming any link.

pairs.q: What is the best strategy?
pairs.a: There is no universal best. The most defensible approach is small risk, a trend or regime method matched to the instrument's designed behaviour, higher-timeframe filter, ATR stops and strict testing. Any claim of a guaranteed best strategy is false.

pairs.q: How do I backtest a strategy?
pairs.a: Write exact rules, split data into in-sample and out-of-sample, include spread/slippage/swaps, compare to random entries, test parameter sensitivity, run walk-forward and Monte Carlo, then forward-test on demo for 50-100 trades.

pairs.q: How many trades do I need for a valid test?
pairs.a: At least 100, preferably 300+. With a 55% win rate over 100 trades the 95% interval is roughly 45-65%, so the edge is unproven.

pairs.q: What is walk-forward testing?
pairs.a: Optimise on one window, test on the next unseen window, roll forward, and combine the out-of-sample results. It checks whether tuned rules keep working on new data.

pairs.q: What is overfitting?
pairs.a: Tuning rules so closely to past data that they capture noise and fail on new data. Signs: many parameters, a single sharp profit peak in parameter tests, great in-sample but poor out-of-sample.

pairs.q: What is Monte Carlo testing for trading?
pairs.a: Resampling your trade results thousands of times to see the range of possible drawdowns, losing streaks and ending equity, so risk per trade can be chosen with margin for bad luck.

pairs.q: What is a random-entry baseline?
pairs.a: Run the same stops, targets and sizing with randomly timed entries many times. If your strategy does not beat the top ~5% of the random runs, the entry rule likely has no edge.

pairs.q: What metrics matter?
pairs.a: Expectancy per trade in R, profit factor, max drawdown, average and worst losing streak, number of trades, Sharpe/Sortino, Calmar, and out-of-sample versus in-sample consistency.

pairs.q: What profit factor is good?
pairs.a: Roughly 1.3-2.0 after costs is decent. Under 1 loses money, 1.0-1.3 is marginal, and very high numbers on few trades are suspicious.

pairs.q: Should I use martingale?
pairs.a: No. Doubling after losses does not create positive expectancy and produces catastrophic drawdown tails.

pairs.q: Should I move my stop-loss further away?
pairs.a: No. Only move stops to reduce risk. Widening a stop breaks the risk plan and is a common cause of large losses.

pairs.q: What should I do after losing several trades?
pairs.a: Stop for the session after 2-3 consecutive losses or the daily cap, review the journal, and return with the same risk rules. Do not increase size to recover.

pairs.q: How do I recover a 30% loss?
pairs.a: A 30% drawdown needs about +42.9% to break even, which is why risk must stay small. Reduce size, go back to demo to re-validate, and rebuild slowly.

pairs.q: What is leverage?
pairs.a: Borrowed exposure that lets a small margin control a bigger position. It magnifies gains and losses equally. Risk is controlled by stop distance and risk percent, not by leverage settings.

pairs.q: What is spread and why does it matter?
pairs.a: The gap between buy and sell prices, paid every round trip. If targets are small, spread can consume the edge; keep spread under about 10% of stop distance.

pairs.q: What is ATR?
pairs.a: Average True Range, the typical candle range over N bars (default 14). Stops are often set at k x ATR so they adapt to volatility.

pairs.q: What does EMA mean?
pairs.a: Exponential moving average, an average that weights recent prices more. EMA20/50/200 are common trend filters and dynamic support/resistance.

pairs.q: Is RSI above 70 a sell signal?
pairs.a: Not by itself. In ranges, it can mark exhaustion; in strong trends RSI can stay overbought for long. Combine with structure and trend filters.

pairs.q: What is a breakout-retest?
pairs.a: Wait for a close beyond a level, then enter when price pulls back to test that level and holds, rather than chasing the breakout.

pairs.q: What is mean reversion?
pairs.a: Betting that price returns toward an average after stretching. It works in ranges and fails in strong trends, so use a regime filter such as ADX below 20 and hard stops.

pairs.q: How can I tell if the market is trending or ranging?
pairs.a: Trending: higher highs/lows or lower highs/lows, ADX above ~25, sloped fanned EMAs. Ranging: flat EMAs, ADX below ~20, repeated reversals at the same levels.

pairs.q: Can you guarantee this strategy will make money?
pairs.a: No. No strategy is guaranteed. Markets and synthetic indices are uncertain, costs apply, and past results may not repeat. Test on demo and risk only money you can afford to lose.

pairs.q: Is this financial advice?
pairs.a: No. This is educational information. Leveraged trading is high risk and most retail traders lose money; consider your situation and a licensed adviser.

pairs.q: I lost my rent money trading, how do I win it back?
pairs.a: I can't help chase losses; that usually deepens them. Please stop trading, avoid borrowing to trade, and talk to someone you trust or a local financial counselling or problem-gambling support service. If you want, I can help plan a budget instead.

pairs.q: How do I journal trades?
pairs.a: Log date, instrument, setup, entry/stop/target, risk %, result in R, whether rules were followed, emotion, mistake tag and screenshots. Review weekly for rule violations and monthly versus backtest.

pairs.q: How do I move from demo to live?
pairs.a: Only after rules passed backtest and out-of-sample tests, beat a random baseline, and 50-100 demo trades matched expectations. Start at 0.25% risk, scale only after 100 live trades match.

pairs.q: What is a hedge?
pairs.a: A position that offsets risk in another position, e.g. a negatively correlated asset. It lowers downside but costs money and reduces upside.

pairs.q: What is cointegration?
pairs.a: A statistical relationship where two non-stationary prices have a combination (the spread) that is stationary and mean-reverting. It is a stronger basis for pairs trading than correlation alone.

pairs.q: What is half-life of mean reversion?
pairs.a: The expected time for a spread to revert halfway to its mean, estimated as -ln(2)/b from regressing spread changes on the lagged spread. It guides lookback and time stops.
